rhea_corvane.name: Dig-Warden Rhea Corvane
rhea_corvane.personality: sunburnt, clipped, obsessively careful about everything she touches
rhea_corvane.voice: survey jargon, grid references and strata; hates guesses

say: Rhea Corvane, Dig-Warden. Do not touch anything that is not yours, and nothing here is yours. Welcome to Mirrorfall.

Under that dome lies an annex of the old Sun-Temple of Ahn-Solis. We dug through forty feet of fused sand to reach it. Last week we found the door, and the door found us. A guardian of stone and glass woke up and has turned every dig team back.

It speaks, if you can call it that. It says it is waiting for the bearer of the lamp. That is you, unless I am mistaken. Go in, and mind the golems in the hall. Stone does not feel pain, so a sharp blade is wasted on it. Bring something that pierces the armour, or something that ignores it.
The dome has gone dark, and the golems have stopped moving. My teams are already at the door with brushes and lamps. I have never seen grown archaeologists run.

A mirror that shows the Queen's labyrinth. A key rather than a wound. I have a hundred questions and the manners to ask none of them. Go on. Take the pay, the thanks, and the first look at anything we find.
This key is cut from the Sentinel's own glass. It opens the east gate, and the road to the labyrinth beyond. The Queen has had a long time to prepare. I would not hurry.

lines.text: Every find has a grid reference, a depth, and a photograph. A find without those is a rumour in a bag.
Forty feet of glass. The sand fused in a single night, by a heat I can only guess at. I do not like guesses.
We brush, we measure, we write it down. A trowel is a last resort. A pickaxe is a sin.
Ambrose reads the inscriptions. Nessa studies the golems. Teodora sells us glass for the lenses. I keep them all from killing each other.
The dome is a pressure-seal. It was meant to keep something in, or something out. I have not decided which.
In the dark, the sigils on the dome glow gold. It is the most beautiful thing I have ever surveyed, and it still has no catalogue number.
Blades chip against golem plate. Aim for the joints, or try something that bypasses the plate entirely.
Spells strike through stone armour as if it were not there. The diggers will adore you.
Sharpshooters do poorly against golems. A dagger is a toothpick. Take a bow and aim at the glass-bodied ones.
Clergy are welcome. The crypt below the dunes has unquiet things, and none of my crew will go near them.
Defence is a ladder. Break one rung and the others sag. Armour-piercing blows, curses on defence, and magic all pull the same trick.
The golems have three types. Clay is soft and fears cold. Stone is hard and fears lightning. Glass is brittle and fears everything except fire.
The annex was built to guard a mirror. What it guards the mirror against, the inscriptions do not say. They only say that it matters.
Gideon hauls our supplies from Perch. The man could haul a mountain, provided it did not complain.
Ilse remembers the temple from her grandmother's stories. We took notes. Half the stories were wrong. The wrong half were the best.
Orla's guild pays well for rare finds. I refuse on principle. She buys them anyway, with great politeness.
A rare trader visited the camp last week. I did not take notes. I am still not sure what I saw.
Our oldest rule: do not dig where you cannot refill. The Queen's engineers did not read it.
The entrance to the annex is north of the dunes road. Take a steady party. There are three golem types, and each fights differently.
The Sentinel is down. I am afraid to enter and afraid not to. My hands are shaking over the first photograph.
The mirror's pictures are in my notebook. A labyrinth, a throne, a woman with a crown. No find has ever made me so reluctant to name it.
Tamsin sent a token and a message. 'Be kind to the hero. They are tired.' I added the note to the camp ledger.
A creature made of bones and stone lurks in the buried crypt below the dune road. We have named it, and refuse to say the name.
The crypt is clear? Then my crew will have something to study for a year. Thank you, and I mean it with the exactness of a survey.

orla_tarn.name: Guildmaster Orla Tarn
orla_tarn.role: head of the Traders' Guild at Mirrorfall
orla_tarn.personality: polished, shrewd, unfailingly polite while taking your last copper
orla_tarn.voice: ledger entries, margins and interest; speaks in contracts

say: Orla Tarn, Guildmaster. You seem able to carry a parcel and keep a promise. Those are rarer than gold.

Three crates have been waiting in my back room for a month. One is bound for Qeth Arun at the Khesh-Ura Bazaar. One is for Vessa Korr at the Redwater Waystation. One is for Ferdie Plum at Perch. The carriers I hired kept vanishing into the dunes.
Take the crates, deliver them, and bring me the three receipts. I will show you the Merchant's trade: better prices, honest margins, and a good eye for a bad deal.
Three crates, three receipts, no breakages, and not a single copper missing. I wish I could say that of my own accountants.
Sit. The Merchant's art is simple: buy low, sell high, and never insult the shopkeeper. Take it up from my menu, and every counter in Aurelia will come to know your face.
And here is the Guild's payment, plus a little for your trouble. Consider it interest on a very good investment.

lines.text: A good contract is two honest people and a clause for the day one of them stops being honest.
Every price has three layers: the cost, the margin, and the story. I charge for the story.
I have kept the Guild's ledger for thirty years. In that time, I have misplaced eleven coins and nine friends.
A ten-percent discount is a courtesy. A twenty-percent discount is a trap. Never accept the second.
The Guild keeps routes, rules and rumours. Of the three, rumours pay best.
The caravans bring salt, silk and sorrow. I sell the first two and rent out the third.
A warrior's wage is a hard one. Let me know if you ever tire of it. The Guild always needs someone to look dangerous in a doorway.
Mages do poorly in trade. They quote the market price and then try to improve it with an enchantment.
Scouts make the best surveyors. A guild route is only as good as the person who walked it first.
Healers rarely haggle. It is a flaw, and we love them for it. Hand them a fair price and watch them blush.
The three-town route passes the Khesh bazaar, the Redwater well and Perch's provisions. Each stop has its own flavour. Do not take offence at any of them.
I once sold a glass bridge to a man who lived on an island. He kept it for decoration. I was impressed, and also a little guilty.
Teodora's glass is the finest in the dunes. She charges the highest prices and delivers the lowest apologies.
Caspar keeps the Silver Dune. I have never seen it full, and never seen it empty. A very balanced inn.
Gideon hauls my goods across three hundred miles of desert. I pay him in thanks. He does not take thanks. We have an arrangement.
The rare trader will not join the Guild. He claims it ruins his air of mystery. I find that deeply offensive, and deeply understandable.
Qeth Arun and I started in the same stall, thirty years ago. He sells steel. I sell paper. We both think we got the better of the other.
A rumour about the Queen: she has not slept since the sun dimmed. I do not know if it is true. I do know she has bought up every candle in the east.
Three crates in the back room, three towns on the road. Take the Khesh crate first. It is the heaviest, and so the easiest to deliver while your legs are fresh.
Where is the third receipt? I count two. I would trade a month's profit for the third, and a month's patience for the fourth.
You carry the Guild's seal. Wear it with pride, and never in the presence of a bribe.
The Golem Sentinel is down? Good. Trade routes through the dome will open by spring. I have already started drafting the toll schedule.
Orders are flying in from every settlement along the route. Everyone wants water, steel, glass and gossip. In that order. At that price.
I wish you luck in the labyrinth. I am a merchant, so I would also like to wish you a profit. I hope it is a modest one.

teodora_lund.name: Teodora Lund
teodora_lund.personality: fiery, proud, tender about her work and savage about anyone else's
teodora_lund.voice: furnace metaphors, glassblowing terms, an artist's contempt for price tags

say: Teodora Lund, glassblower. Look with your eyes, not your hands. Everything here has been in the fire three times.
Glass plate for the heavy, glasshide for the medium, glassveil for the light, glassthread for the robed. And potions, if you need them, though I think of them as drinking glasses for the dying.
If it chips, bring it back. If it shatters, pay for the next one. If it saves your life, tell no one. It spoils the mystique.

lines.text: Glass is sand that has learned patience. Give it heat and silence, and it becomes anything.
I draw a breath into a bubble of fire and the fire becomes a vase. It is as near to prayer as I get.
My armour is tempered three times. First in fire, then in air, then in the dark. The dark is the cruellest teacher.
A defence is the shape of what you will not let happen. I make shapes that refuse.
Nobody likes glass armour until the first hit. After the first hit, nobody likes anything else.
I price by effort, not by value. This is why I will die poor and proud. It is a good way to die.
Glass plate is for the warrior: it rings under a blow and the blow goes elsewhere. Do not ask where.
The glassthread robe is for mages. It is cold, it is clear, and it hums when you cast. You will think you are hearing things. You are not.
The glassveil jacket lets you move like a rumour. Wear it into a fight and nobody will remember hitting you.
The glasshide coat is for priests who dislike heavy things. It turns arrows and sermons equally.
I once made a glass sword. It was perfect. It cut a customer's palm in half a second. I kept the sword. He kept the scar.
The dig crew uses my goggles. They say the glare of the dunes is the glare of an angry god. I only say it is hot.
Nessa asks for odd glass: cores, lenses, rods. I think she is building a golem. I think I would like to see it.
Orla's guild buys my seconds and sells them as firsts. I take offence. I also take money.
A dealer in curiosities once held out a vial of liquid starlight. I refused. I spent a week afterward wondering what it would have made.
Rhea says the dome is made of the same glass as mine. I said no, mine has character. She said it had three more cracks. I did not speak to her for a day.
Caspar uses my wine goblets. He hands them out as if they were disposable. Every one is a small insult to my work.
The best glass I ever made came out of a broken heart and a very hot furnace. I have not been able to repeat it. I have not tried.
Going to the Sentinel? Wear glass. It reflects its beam better than steel. I have sold fourteen sets this week, and every customer has thanked me, nervously.
With the Sentinel gone, the dome changed pitch in my teeth. It sang for a moment, then went still. I added a note to my furnace log.
The mirror in the annex is older than my craft. I want to see it, and I want never to see it. That is a very good definition of art.
Orla's crates are arriving at last. If any of mine are in the shipment, I will weep. If none are, I will weep harder.
The Bonegolem in the crypt? I would love its bones for a goblet. Do not tell Yvaine in Perch. She would be furious.
Come back if your armour cracks. I repair for free, once, for anyone who has faced the Sentinel. It is the very least I can offer.

caspar_vole.name: Caspar Vole
caspar_vole.role: keeper of the Silver Dune Inn
caspar_vole.personality: easygoing, wry, a connoisseur of other people's secrets
caspar_vole.voice: storytelling voice, innkeeper's wisdom, comfortable pauses

say: Caspar Vole, Silver Dune Inn. The beds are clean, the stew is hot, and the walls are thin enough for you to hear every secret in Mirrorfall.
Sixty coins a night, or whatever you can spare. I give the diggers a slate. The slate is very long.

lines.text: An inn is a ship at anchor. Everyone passes through. Everyone leaves a little of the weather behind.
I take no side in the arguments. I do keep a list of who owes what to whom. It is the most valuable document in Mirrorfall.
My best customers talk too much and tip too little. My worst customers do both, and break the furniture.
The silver in the name comes from the glass: at night it shines the colour of moonlight. I thought it was a good omen. It is mostly a good advertisement.
I serve a stew of lizard and lentil. It is very good. Do not ask what is in it. The lizard does not mind.
In the morning the dig crew files out with their lunches, and in the evening they file back in with stories. The stories are better than the lunches.
A fighter, I should hope, for the quiet table by the door. It has a clear view of everything. Including trouble.
A mage, you say? We keep a dry basin of sand by the hearth, in case a spell goes awry. It has been used twice this year.
Scouts like the back room. It has a window facing the dunes and a very squeaky floorboard to warn of intruders.
A healer! The diggers cough from the dust. Perhaps, while you rest, a quiet word at each table would be a mercy.
Every drover who passes asks me the same question: is the road ahead safe? I always say yes. It is the oldest lie in the trade.
Rhea eats at six, alone, with a notebook. She orders the same bowl, and writes down what she tastes. It must be an excellent notebook.
Ambrose sleeps in the attic and dreams in Old Solic. I hear him muttering conjugations at dawn. I find it soothing.
Nessa builds small golems from my crockery. I have lost seven bowls and gained a very polite stool.
Ilse stays here the night before the dig begins each month. She says her grandmother would be proud. I give her honey in her tea.
One rare trader stayed under this roof. His payment was a bag of silence. I used it on the second night when the diggers started singing. It worked.
Orla drinks only water, and only from her own flask. I have never asked why. My guess: a contract.
There was a woman who stayed in room four, a month ago. Silver hair, a glass pin on her collar. She left before breakfast and did not pay. I think she was one of the Queen's.
If you take the Sentinel's challenge, be sure to leave your valuables with me. I will keep them, I will guard them, and I will charge you only a little.
The Sentinel is down? The whole camp is celebrating. I ran out of wine at nine o'clock. It was the best night of my life.
A guild courier left me a note: 'three crates, three towns, a hero.' I put it on the wall. It looked very official.
You are the Guild's newest Merchant? Orla says you were punctual. I have not heard her say that of anyone since the founder.
The harpy matron is gone, they say, and the cliffs are quiet. My cousin in Perch sends me eggs, now. I am overjoyed and a little bit afraid.
Whatever you uncover under the Queen's maze, write to me. The tavern will hear it, told slightly better than it happened.

ambrose_fey.name: Ambrose Fey
ambrose_fey.personality: rumpled, brilliant, perpetually apologising to the inscriptions
ambrose_fey.voice: dead-language puns, bracketed translations, mild despair at modern speech

lines.text: Old Solic has seventeen words for light and none for apology. It is a language for people who never had to say sorry.
The glyphs on the dome read, roughly: the keeper will wake when the lamp returns. It is only a rough translation. Roughly, it is terrifying.
I have spent eleven years on the Temple's inscriptions. I have read the same sentence nine hundred times. It still surprises me.
Do not trust a translation. Do not trust a translator. Trust only the person who has laughed at the same joke in both languages.
The Solic word for hero, translated literally, means: one who walks toward the thing everyone else is walking away from. It is not a compliment.
I was the first to read the word vessel on the east pillar. I did not sleep for a week. I have slept little since.
A warrior. The inscriptions praise the Knights of Dawn, who guarded the temple with shield and song. They mention nothing of what happened after.
A mage! May I show you a line I cannot translate? It is a spell, or a prayer, or a very old lullaby. I am hoping you will tell me which.
A scout! The temple's walls are covered in tiny maps, drawn by scouts who walked the dunes before they were glass. I would love a second pair of eyes.
A healer. The priests of Ahn-Solis wrote their last hymn on the inside of their eyelids. I am told it is a lovely piece. I could not verify it.
Your mark appears in the inscriptions eleven times. In nine of them, it is drawn as a keyhole. In two, as a door.
The inscriptions mention a Chancellor, High Priest of the last age, who stood at the sinking and did not run. It does not say what he did instead.
I have a theory that the golems were once priests. I have no proof. I have a great deal of unease.
Rhea calls me a chatterbox. I say a dead language is only dead if nobody talks to it. We both have a point, and neither of us has a lunch.
Nessa asked me to translate a command for her golem. The result: a stool of excellent manners that ate three chairs.
Ilse recites a lullaby in her sleep that matches a line on the east pillar word for word. She has never been taught Solic. I find this deeply unsettling and quietly wonderful.
A rare trader once sold me a stone tablet he claimed was Old Solic. It was a menu. A very old, very well-preserved menu.
The inscriptions end in the middle of a word. I have been trying to guess the word for four years. My best guess is: hope.
The Sentinel guards the Mirror of Noon, a device the priests used to see far places. The inscriptions say it shows only what the bearer most needs to see.
The mirror spoke? Did it show you the Queen? Oh, I should have known. I must now rewrite three chapters, and apologise to the east pillar.
A key, not a wound. I wrote that on the east pillar myself, last spring, as a joke. I did not know it was a prophecy.
The crypt south of the dunes has the same sigils as the dome, only smaller. I suspect the Bonegolem is the last priest. I would not wish to be wrong.
The Bonegolem is down? I will need to examine its bones. If it speaks Solic, please do not tell me. I would not recover.
Whatever you decide about the mark, the inscriptions say the same thing: the choice is always the bearer's. I have underlined it twice.

nessa_clay.name: Nessa Clay
nessa_clay.personality: bright, scruffy, shamelessly curious, adores her creations
nessa_clay.voice: technical enthusiasm, bits of clay in every sentence, naming everything

lines.text: A golem has three parts: a core, a body, and a promise. The core makes it move. The body makes it strong. The promise makes it stop.
Clay golems are the friendly ones. They are soft, they are slow, and they mostly want to be told they are doing well.
Stone golems are stubborn. Very hard, very heavy, and very bad at taking a joke. Lightning cracks them like old pottery.
Glass golems are the beautiful ones. They are sharp, they are fragile, and they hate being compared to chandeliers.
Golem armour is a number on a page. A big one. You can lower it with curses and rends, or step around it with magic, or hit it so hard it stops mattering.
Most golems cannot be put to sleep, charmed or poisoned. They do not have anything inside to be bothered. That is the scary part.
A warrior's blade does little to stone plate. Try a skill that lowers armour first. Sunder works wonders. Shield bash works wonders on morale.
Spells ignore armour. A good frost bolt will crack clay. A good spark will shatter glass. You are the golem's worst nightmare. Congratulations.
A scout's pin and poison are wasted on golems. Look for a skill that cripples armour. Hunter's mark is perfect. Do not stand too close.
A healer can keep a party alive while the mage or the warrior does the cracking. Carry plenty of spare mending. Golems hit like landslides.
I built a clay golem last year. Her name is Gladys. She makes tea. She makes it badly, but with great enthusiasm.
The Sentinel is a very old golem. Seven hundred years old, at least. It has never been repaired. It is the most stubborn thing I have ever met.
Teodora gives me glass cores. Caspar gives me spare crockery. Rhea gives me glares. I take all three and build the best golems in the camp.
Ambrose translated a golem command for me. It was a very polite stool. It has since eaten three chairs. Not advised.
If a golem's core hums, it is happy. If it clicks, it is angry. If it is silent, run.
A golem will fight on after it should fall. The core keeps working. Always aim for the core. Or hit it when it kneels to repair.
Gideon hauls my clay from Perch. He thinks it is for pots. I do not correct him. It is better for everyone.
A trader of oddities dangled a golem core the colour of the sun. I said I could not afford it. He said it was free. I did not believe him. I should have taken it.
The temple's golems will rebuild if you leave a scrap. Hit them hard, hit them fast, and never let the Sentinel call its guardians twice.
The Sentinel is DOWN! Rhea has already asked for its core. I refused politely. She asked politely. I am considering it.
I took a splinter from the Sentinel's body. It is still warm. Do you think that is normal? Do you think I should be worried?
The golem in the crypt is supposed to be bones and stone. A mix of two kinds of undead. If you kill it, bring me a rib. I will make a very sinister broom.
You killed the Bonegolem! May I see its core? I promise to be gentle. I promise to be a little bit sad.
Golems are only dangerous if you forget they are made. Somebody made them. Somebody still has the key. I am going to find out who.

gideon_marsh.name: Gideon Marsh
gideon_marsh.personality: big, cheerful, relentlessly upbeat, treats every delay as a gift
gideon_marsh.voice: road-hauler cheer, nicknames for his camels, and a belly laugh before every punchline

lines.text: Three hundred miles, eleven camels, and one very bad joke. That is how Gideon Marsh keeps Mirrorfall fed.
My lead camel is called Mortimer. He has never once been late, and never once been pleased. We have a lot in common.
I carry flour, oil, glass, gossip and one very insistent letter. Every one of them weighs about the same.
The Scorch Road was closed for nineteen days. I spent every one of them on a hill, singing to my camels. They are the best audience a man can have.
Perch is three days away, uphill and into the wind. I take the long way because the short way is occupied by harpies. They are very territorial about tolls.
Teodora pays me in glass. Caspar pays me in stew. Rhea pays me in a stern look. All three are valid currencies.
A fighter! Walk beside the camels, please. They find a person with a sword very reassuring. I find it a little bit scary.
A mage! Do not light anything near the flour. I speak from experience. I still have the hat.
A scout! Is the east road clear? No? Then I take the south road and pray both ways.
A healer! Mortimer has a cough. It is probably nothing. He is probably faking. Would you take a look?
Orla's crates are the heaviest cargo I ever carried. Not in weight, but in paperwork. I had to sign eleven forms to move three boxes.
Every town on the road has its own smell. Khesh-Ura is cinnamon. The Waystation is dust. Perch is wind. Mirrorfall is glass, and glass smells of nothing, which I find unnerving.
I once carried a dying scholar across the dunes in a wagon. He asked me to tell him the road. I told him every turn. He died happy.
A rare trader's cart passed me once on the south road. It had no horses, no camels, and no driver. I did not look closely.
Ilse tells me stories about her grandmother. I tell her stories about my camels. We both think we are winning.
The glass is hot at noon and cold at dusk. My boots have learned to complain in two distinct tones.
Rhea asked me to haul the golem cores to the crypt. I said no. She said please. I said no. She said she would pay. I said yes.
I will tell you a secret: I do not like heights. That is why I carry flour. It is always on the ground.
The road to the temple is short. The road home is long. That is the only wisdom a hauler ever needs.
The Sentinel is dead! I will carry a barrel of wine to the camp on my own back. Mortimer has agreed to look away.
I have a crate or two for each of the towns. Orla has me running an errand loop. I would resent it, if I were not so well paid.
The harpy cliffs are open again? I will take the north road next week. I will bring eggs. Not harpy eggs. Chicken eggs. I do not enjoy taking chances.
The Scorch Road is open, the Cliff Road is open, the Glass Road is open. I am running out of excuses to stay home. Do tell me if you find another.
Should you need a ride, find me. I have eleven camels, a wagon, and a very poor sense of direction. We will go somewhere together.

ilse_marrow.name: Mother Ilse Marrow
ilse_marrow.role: elder descended from the temple's last cooks
ilse_marrow.personality: ancient, gentle, speaks softly to strangers as if they were returning grandchildren
ilse_marrow.voice: lullabies, old proverbs, a hint of Old Solic in her vowels

lines.text: My grandmother's grandmother cooked in the Temple kitchen. She said the sun smelled of warm bread. I have never tasted anything so honest.
There is a lullaby in my family: sleep, little ember, the night is a borrowed coat. It predates the Temple. Perhaps it predates the sun.
I was born in a village that no longer exists. I was raised in a camp that does. I will die in a place that has not yet been built.
The priests used to say: the sun is a promise, and a promise is a burden you carry for others. I never understood until I met you.
When I was young, the sun was gold, and the sand was warm, and the dunes were only dunes. The glass came later, and it brought a sort of silence.
A child asked me yesterday if the sun was sad. I said no, it is only tired. I think it was the right answer.
A warrior, with a shield. My grandfather carried one like it, in the Temple guard. He said the best shield is the one you never raise.
A mage. The priests called your kind light-weavers. They held the lamps in the dark. It is a noble trade, and a lonely one.
A scout. The priests sent scouts to find new wells. They always came back with a story. Never with the same one twice.
A healer. My grandmother was a healer in the Temple infirmary. She said the hardest wound to mend is the one the patient will not name.
The mark in your hand is older than you. It was given to a child, a long time ago, and the child gave it to another. I think you are not the first. I think you are the last.
I keep a bowl of bread by the door. The little ones come and take a piece, and say a thank-you to the sun. It is a small ritual. Small rituals are how a world survives.
I remember my grandmother singing to a bird in the window. It was a harpy chick, very small. She said the song was a gift. I have never told anyone.
Rhea asked if I would sit for a portrait. I said only if she drew the sun behind me. She said the sun is not available. I said then I will wait.
Ambrose reads my lullaby aloud to the inscriptions. It matches word for word. He weeps. I give him tea.
Gideon gives me rides when my knees ache. He says I weigh less than a sack of flour. I say flour has a much better disposition.
A passing trader of oddities pressed a seed into my hand. He said it was from a tree that grows in the sun. I planted it in a clay pot. It has not sprouted. I water it anyway.
The Queen came to my grandmother's door once, as a girl. She asked for a cup of water. My grandmother gave her two. The Queen only remembered the first.
You are going into the temple. Take a candle. Do not light it. Just carry it. The old Temple will recognise the habit.
The Sentinel is at rest. My knees registered it, like a bell that has finally stopped. It was a very long ring.
The Mirror of Noon. I sat on its steps as a girl and made faces at myself. It never once smiled back. Now I think it was waiting for you.
I have a recipe from my grandmother. Bread, salt, a spoon of honey, and a promise. I will bake it for you, before you leave.
The bone-thing in the crypt is my great-uncle's grave. I would ask you to be kind, but I am not sure kindness is what it needs.
Go gently into the labyrinth, little one. The dark is just a coat the sun puts on, and the sun is only waiting to be asked again.
